meaning: ‘death, the tempter’, the personification of death and desire who assailed the Buddha under the Bodhi tree (from √mṛ ‘to die’), MW.

pronunciation.approximation: MAH-ruh — the ā is long; two syllables, no ornament.
pronunciation.note: Māra derives from √mṛ, "to die" (Monier-Williams): "death, the killer" — the personification of everything that kills the spiritual life, from desire to death itself. The Pāli canon also knows him as Namuci (an old Vedic name), Pāpimā, "the Evil One," and Kaṇha, "the Dark One." The restoration's whole content is the long ā: the difference between "Mara" and Māra is the difference between a name and the word for death. Tier-1 by rule.

kin.label: Vedic antecedent
kin.form: Namuci, the asura of the Ṛgveda slain by Indra

kin.label: His daughters
kin.form: Taṇhā, Aratī, Rāgā — Craving, Aversion, Passion

domains.title: The Tempter
domains.subtitle: The Ten Armies, the Three Daughters, and the Defeat of Being Seen
domains.lead: Māra is Death wearing every disguise the mind can manufacture: the lord of the desire-realm who marched his ten armies against the Buddha under the Bodhi tree, sent his three daughters when the armies broke, and lost — not to a weapon, but to being recognized.

cards.name: The Ten Armies
cards.desc: Lust, discontent, hunger, craving, sloth, fear, doubt, obstinacy, glory, and self-praise — the Sutta Nipāta's catalog.

cards.name: The Three Daughters
cards.desc: Taṇhā, Aratī, Rāgā: Craving, Aversion, Passion — the last seduction, sent when the army fled.

cards.name: Girimekhala
cards.desc: His war-elephant, Mountain-high — which knelt, the commentaries say, when the earth itself bore witness.

cards.name: The Flower-Arrowed Bow
cards.desc: Borrowed from Kāma, the love-god: the weapons of desire — beautiful, flowered, and aimed.

symbols.name: The tenfold army
symbols.meaning: The taxonomy of temptation: every assault on resolve sorted by battalion

symbols.name: The flower arrows
symbols.meaning: Desire's camouflage: the shafts that arrive looking like gifts

symbols.name: The shadow at the seat
symbols.meaning: His claim on the Bodhi throne: the ego's final argument, "this place is mine"

symbols.name: The deva of the Vasavattī heaven
symbols.meaning: Māra is no devil from below but a god of the highest desire-realm — the ceiling of saṃsāra, himself subject to the wheel; his terror is that even the tempter ends

mythology.lead: Māra's mythology is the dark half of the Buddhist biography: wherever the teaching advances, the texts station him at the next bend — and his defeats chart the whole path from striving to parinibbāna.

myths.title: The Ten Armies
myths.text: The Sutta Nipāta's Padhāna Sutta gives his order of battle, and it is a psychology textbook disguised as an epic: sensual pleasure is the first army, discontent the second, hunger and thirst the third, craving the fourth, sloth and torpor the fifth, fear the sixth, doubt the seventh, hypocrisy and obstinacy the eighth, gains, fame, and honor the ninth, and the tenth — the general's own guard — is self-exaltation joined with contempt for others. Māra rides the elephant Girimekhala, a hundred leagues tall, and boasts that not even a thousand Sakyans together could escape him. The Buddha's answer opens the whole tradition's arsenal: 'I see your army, Kāma, arrayed all around; I shall go forth against it, and it shall not shake me.' He names each battalion as it advances and walks through the camp untouched. The catalog is Buddhism's map of the inner war, and its thesis is exact: every assault on resolve is a known quantity — recognition is resistance, and resistance is victory. No sūtra equips the Buddha with a weapon; none has ever been needed.

myths.title: The Night Under the Tree
myths.text: The full assault is told in the Nidānakathā and versified in Aśvaghoṣa's Buddhacarita, whose thirteenth canto — the Defeat of Māra — is Sanskrit poetry's great set-piece: whirlwinds that cannot stir the bodhisattva's robe, a rain of rocks that falls as garlands, darkness that will not spread, a flight of arrows that turns to flowers before it lands. Mounted on Girimekhala, Māra advances his final claim — the seat of awakening is his by right of lineage and merit — and calls his army as witness. The bodhisattva answers with the gesture that defines Buddhist art: he reaches down and touches the earth, and the earth itself, summoned as witness to his perfections, thunders back. The elephant kneels; the host scatters; the dawn comes up on an undefeated man. The scene's theology is the entire soteriology in one image: truth is not argued into being but ratified by reality, and evil's weapons decompose on contact with a mind that has stopped debating and simply knows.

myths.title: The Daughters
myths.text: Force having failed, Māra sent subtlety: his three daughters, Taṇhā (Craving), Aratī (Aversion), and Rāgā (Passion), came to the newly-awakened Buddha in every guise beauty can wear — maiden, mother, worker, queen — and made their offer one after another. He regarded each in turn and dismissed her with the calm of a man reading names off a list: 'I have done with craving; go, daughters, find your husbands elsewhere.' The Saṃyutta Nikāya's whole Māra cycle ends nearly every one of these duels the same way — with the Tempter's signature lament: 'The Blessed One knows me; the Fortunate One knows me.' It is the most repeated sentence of defeat in any scripture: to be seen is to be beaten. His daughters never stop being born — every desire the mind produces wears their three faces in rotation — but the text's point stands untouched: the disguise is the only power temptation has, and recognition strips it bare.

myths.title: The Last Visit
myths.text: Māra keeps one appointment to the very end. In the Mahāparinibbāna Sutta he comes to the aged Buddha at Beluvagāmaka, and — the text is deliciously precise — he comes not with armies but with a calendar: reminding the Blessed One of his ancient promise, that he would not pass away into final nirvana until the four assemblies — monks, nuns, laymen, laywomen — were well established in the practice. That work is done now; it is time. And the Buddha, who once broke his army by seeing him, grants the request without resistance: in three months, at Vesālī, the Tathāgata will pass away. The tradition's point is exact and unsettling — the tempter's only final success is the world's impermanence keeping its schedule. Māra did not win; he was merely the messenger of a deadline that includes him. Even the lord of death is a mortal god, and his three months' notice is the sūtra's last joke at his expense.

lore.syncretism: His oldest document is Vedic: Namuci, the asura of the Ṛgveda whom Indra slew with the foam of the waters, survived in the Pāli canon as Māra's other name — a borrowing as old as the texts themselves. Indian religion lent him Kāma's iconography, the sugarcane bow and flower arrows of the love-god, for desire was his first army. The scholastics then multiplied him: the Mahāyāna handbooks count four Māras — the aggregates, the defilements, death, and the god — turning the tempter into a complete theory of bondage. And the comparison with Satan, inevitable since the first missionaries, is inexact in the instructive way: Māra is no eternal adversary but a god of the highest desire-realm heaven, the Vasavattī, himself mortal, himself subject to the wheel — the ceiling of samsāra, not its enemy.
lore.culturalLegacy: Māra gave Buddhism its psychology of the inner adversary: modern teachers from forest masters to mindfulness clinicians read the ten armies as the mind's own defenses against stillness, and "the Blessed One knows me" as the moment every compulsion loses power — when it is seen. His assault is the most-painted scene in Buddhist art, from Gandhāran panels to the murals of a thousand Thai wats, where the earth-goddess Thoranī wrings a flood from her hair to drown his host. And his name still does its original work: in the teaching languages of three continents, māra remains the common noun for what kills.
lore.extendedMeditation: Māra is the only adversary who is defeated exclusively by being identified. No sūtra has the Buddha out-argue him, out-pray him, or out-fight him: he is seen, and he is finished — "I see you, Māra" — and his own epitaph is "the Blessed One knows me." Every craving, every fear, every vanity keeps his treaty: unnamed, it commands; named, it kneels like Girimekhala. The tradition offers no other weapon because none has ever been needed.
lore.archaeology: The assault on the Bodhi seat is among the oldest narrative scenes in Buddhist art: Gandhāran schist panels of the first centuries CE — now in Peshawar, Lahore, and Western collections — show the demon host shrinking from the seated figure, and the Pāla-period steles of the eight great events put the Māra-vijaya at the center of the sacred biography. The bhūmisparśa image that records the victory became the default Buddha of mainland Southeast Asia; Thai, Lao, and Khmer temple murals added the earth-goddess Thoranī wringing the flood from her hair; and Bodh Gayā itself — the vajrāsana, the "diamond throne" beneath the descendant of the very tree — remains the one site on earth where his defeat has a postal address.
